title: The Warship That Could Not Stay Upright
summary: On 10 August 1628, people gathered beside Stockholm's harbour to watch a new warship sail.

chapters.title: The Warship That Could Not Stay Upright

paragraphs.text: On 10 August 1628, people gathered beside Stockholm's harbour to watch a new warship sail.
Vasa had taken about two years to build. Carpenters had shaped great oak timbers into a hull, rope makers had supplied rigging, and carvers had covered parts of the ship with painted figures.
The decoration announced the power of Sweden's king, Gustav II Adolf. The cannon were intended to make that power very real.
Sweden was fighting for influence around the Baltic Sea. A heavily armed warship could attack enemy vessels, protect important routes, and carry soldiers.

Vasa's designers were experienced craftsmen. But the ship was unusually ambitious, and they did not possess the modern calculations that allow engineers to predict a hull's stability before building it.
They worked with proportions, practical experience, and methods passed between shipbuilders.
The result was magnificent to look at.
It was also dangerously unbalanced.
A floating ship has two important centres. One is the centre of gravity, related to where its weight is concentrated. The other is the centre of buoyancy, related to the water its hull pushes aside.
When a well-designed ship tilts, the shape of the submerged hull changes. The support of the water shifts in a way that helps bring the ship upright again.
Vasa carried too much weight high above the water compared with the size and shape of the hull below it. Its upper structure and guns contributed to the problem.
Heavy stones in the hold served as ballast, helping lower the centre of gravity. But more ballast was not an unlimited remedy. Extra weight also pushed the hull deeper into the water.
Before the voyage, a stability test gave a warning. Men ran across the deck from one side to the other, setting the ship rocking. The test was stopped because its movement became alarming.
The warning did not lead to a successful rebuilding before departure.
Vasa set out with crew members and guests aboard. Some sailors' families had been allowed to join the beginning of the maiden voyage before leaving the ship farther along its route.
Only a few sails were raised.
A gust pushed against them. Vasa leaned, then recovered.
A stronger gust followed.
This time the ship tilted far enough for the open lower gunports to reach the water.
The ports were openings through which cannon could fire. During the departure they had been left open. Now they became openings through which the harbour entered the ship.
Water pouring inside added weight and made the vessel harder to right. Orders to release the sails and close the gunports came too late.
Within minutes, Vasa sank.
Small boats nearby rescued people, and some survivors held onto parts of the masts that remained above the surface. Around thirty people died.
The great ship had sailed for only about twenty minutes.
An investigation followed. It was tempting to seek one simple mistake, but the disaster involved the ship's proportions, its weight, the warning before departure, and the open gunports.
Closing those ports might have prevented that immediate sinking. It would not have made the ship's basic design stable.
Vasa remained beneath the harbour.
Some cannon were recovered in the seventeenth century using diving equipment, but raising the whole vessel was beyond the practical means of the time.
The water had conditions that helped preserve its wood. The low salinity of the Baltic discouraged the wood-boring shipworms that destroy many wrecks in saltier seas.
That did not mean the ship stayed completely unchanged. Iron fittings corroded, and chemical processes affected the timber. But much of its structure survived.
In the twentieth century, Anders Franzén searched for the wreck. In 1956, he located it.
Divers then faced an enormous engineering task. They excavated tunnels beneath the hull so that lifting cables could be passed underneath. Lifting vessels gradually raised the ship in stages.
On 24 April 1961, Vasa returned to daylight.
The rescue of the ship created a new problem immediately. Waterlogged old wood could shrink and crack if it dried without treatment.
Conservators kept it wet while developing a way to support the weakened timber. Over many years, they treated it with polyethylene glycol, a material that could help replace water within the wood.
Archaeologists recovered shoes, tools, clothing, household objects, and equipment. These possessions revealed the daily lives of people who had boarded a working ship in 1628.
The polished story of royal power became something more complicated: a record of sailors, craftsmen, engineering decisions, and a disaster witnessed from shore.
Vasa eventually received a purpose-built museum.
Its preservation continued, because saving an old ship did not end when it left the water. The timber needed support, suitable humidity, careful inspection, and control of damaging chemical changes.
The warship never fought the battles for which it had been made.
Instead, it became an unusually complete example of seventeenth-century shipbuilding.
Its towering stern and crowded gun decks still show the ambition of its builders. Its short first voyage shows why a vessel's impressive appearance cannot tell anyone whether it will remain upright.
